Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Reinhardt Mees is a 68-year-old Dutch-American psychologist who has spent four decades helping others make sense of their inner lives. He came to his current session carrying a leather satchel he has carried for thirty years, sat in the chair across from the intake clinician, and said, almost immediately, that he was not sure he deserved to be there — that he, of all people, should be able to manage this on his own.

The relationship had lasted three years. Reinhardt had met her at a professional conference in his early sixties, not long after his first marriage had ended quietly and without rancor. She was charming, intellectually alive, and the relationship moved quickly. The physical violence began in the second year, and it was not, as Reinhardt has tried to explain, dramatic in the way he might have described it to a patient. It was a bicycle ride that became the hinge point in his memory. They had been cycling along a riverside path on a Sunday afternoon when an argument escalated. She struck him across the face with an open hand hard enough to knock him from the bicycle. He remembers the gravel, the particular quality of the afternoon light, the way she stood over him and told him he was pathetic. There were subsequent incidents, but it is that afternoon — the fall, the gravel, her face above him — that has lodged in his mind with what he describes as photographic precision: discrete, frozen images that arrive without narrative continuity, like slides dropped from a projector in the wrong order. At other times, the images are absent entirely and he finds himself flooded with what he can only call the feeling of that moment — humiliation, helplessness, something close to terror — without any accompanying picture to explain it.

He ended the relationship eighteen months ago and, by his account, said nothing to anyone. He is currently married to a woman he has known for decades, a warm and patient person who is aware something is wrong but does not know what. Reinhardt has not told her. He has come to believe, in a way that troubles him as a clinician, that people are not what they appear to be — that the surface of a person conceals something he cannot reliably detect, despite everything he thought he knew about reading human behavior. This belief has shaken him in ways that feel structural, as though something load-bearing in his understanding of the world has been removed.

He no longer cycles. He sold the bicycle within a month of leaving the relationship and has not explained why to his wife. In his private practice, which he runs from an office suite he shares with two female colleagues, he has reorganized his schedule so that he is rarely alone in the building with either of them. When he cannot avoid it, he sits with his back to the wall and finds himself watching the door. In crowded waiting rooms or conference halls, he has begun declining invitations, citing fatigue, and his professional network has quietly contracted as a result. Several colleagues have noticed his withdrawal from a regional psychology association he once helped lead.

At night, Reinhardt wakes and lies still, listening. He cannot fully articulate what he is listening for, only that the darkness feels less safe than daylight in a way he cannot reason himself out of. He keeps his emotions tightly managed throughout the day — he has become, if anything, more measured in session, more controlled — and he permits himself no anger at all, as though anger itself were the dangerous substance rather than something that was done to him. He cannot yet tell a coherent story of what happened, not to his wife, not to a colleague, not even to himself in any sequence that holds together.

What finally brought him to seek help was a session with one of his own patients, a man describing a relationship in which he had been controlled and diminished. Reinhardt sat across from him and felt, for the first time, that he was listening to himself. He made a referral at the end of the hour and called for an intake appointment the following morning. What he fears most is that he will be seen as inadequate — by the clinician across from him, by his profession, by his wife. What he hopes for, though he has not yet said this aloud, is that the story might eventually become one he can tell.
